name: Scheele's Green
poem: A dazzling arsenic green that coloured wallpaper, dresses and sweets — and is rumoured to have slowly killed Napoleon in exile.

recipe.note: A strong leaf green, warmed slightly with yellow.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: The first really brilliant green available to oil painters — and one that quietly poisoned everyone who handled it.

entries.title: The Café Terrace at Night
entries.blurb: Van Gogh's bottle greens are largely copper-arsenite pigments — Scheele's green and its successors. The colour glowed; the painter's mental decline accelerated.

entries.title: Cézanne's Still Lifes
entries.blurb: The deep leaf greens of Cézanne's apples and pears were often Scheele's — by the time he switched to viridian, decades of skin contact had already happened.

entries.title: Victorian Botanical Plates
entries.blurb: Hand-coloured botanical illustrations almost universally used Scheele's green — the only pigment that could match real foliage. Colourists died young.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: The most fashionable colour in the Victorian wardrobe — and a leading cause of mysterious deaths among the people who wore it.

entries.title: The Ballroom Gown
entries.blurb: A Scheele's-green silk evening dress could shed enough arsenic dust over a single night to kill the wearer's dance partner. Coroners began to suspect.

entries.title: Artificial Flowers
entries.blurb: Hat makers' assistants in London brushed arsenic green powder onto silk leaves all day. Reports describe pale girls vomiting green into the gutter outside.

entries.title: Children's Toys
entries.blurb: Wooden rocking horses, painted dolls, even children's books were finished in arsenic green — colour-fast, weather-proof, untested for toxicity in the mouth.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Real leaves get their green from chlorophyll, not arsenic — but Scheele's green was made because chlorophyll fades and arsenic doesn't.

entries.title: Spring Foliage
entries.blurb: The exact green of beech leaves in early May — fresh enough to look almost synthetic. Scheele was trying to bottle this, and he very nearly did.

entries.title: Arsenic Ore
entries.blurb: The mineral source — arsenic appears in nature as bright yellow and red ores. Reacting it with copper and acid produces Scheele's green.

entries.title: Algae Blooms
entries.blurb: Modern algae blooms turn lakes the same vivid green as Scheele's pigment — and are often as toxic. Both kill quietly, by ingestion.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: Scheele's green is the rare pigment with its own murder mystery — and a contested cause of death for an emperor.

entries.title: Napoleon at Longwood
entries.blurb: Napoleon's exile bedroom was papered in Scheele's-green wallpaper. Damp tropical air liberated arsenic vapour. His hair samples confirm: lethal levels.

entries.title: The Killer Wallpaper
entries.blurb: An estimated 100 million square feet of arsenic-green wallpaper hung in Victorian Britain. Children's bedrooms were a leading site of unexplained illness.

entries.title: "Bitter Tasting Sweets"
entries.blurb: A confectioner accidentally mixed Scheele's green into a batch of peppermint humbugs instead of sugar — twenty-one children died, fifty were severely poisoned.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: The pigment was named, like several others in the era, for the chemist who first synthesised it — Carl Wilhelm Scheele had a talent for discovering deadly things.

entries.title: Carl Wilhelm Scheele
entries.blurb: Scheele discovered oxygen, chlorine, and seven other elements — and died at 43, probably from tasting his own discoveries. The green was an afterthought.

entries.title: "Copper Arsenite"
entries.blurb: The chemical name — produced by combining copper sulfate with sodium arsenite. A pale yellow-green powder until exposed to acid, which intensifies the colour.

entries.title: "Schweinfurt Green"
entries.blurb: A copper-arsenoacetate variant developed in Schweinfurt — brighter, more stable, even more toxic. Sold under both names interchangeably for a century.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Scheele's green became the colour of progress made before its consequences were understood — the 19th century's perfect pigment for itself.

entries.title: Decadence
entries.blurb: Oscar Wilde reportedly furnished his lodgings in arsenic green — the colour came to symbolise late-Victorian decadence, beautiful and a little doomed.

entries.title: The Gothic Revival
entries.blurb: Walls of Scheele's green made every gas-lit Gothic Revival parlour look like the inside of a forest at midnight — a colour for ghost stories.

entries.title: Death in Beauty
entries.blurb: Scheele's green is the leading example of a recurring pigment story: a colour too lovely to refuse, even after the deaths start adding up.
